Under it, a description of the axis, one sentence at each end."LLM Decides the Next Step" · "No Step to Decide" · "Agent Decides Everything"Jun's Speech• Why this slide: the audience already has several AI tools within reach. This gives them a map of what each tool is, what it is good for, and where RiskMind sits, before we introduce RiskMind.
• Two kinds of tools, split by one question: can the tool run multiple steps? Chat is on the left and Agentic Systems is on the right. A vertical dashed line separates them.
• Picture the axis as a slider: how freely the LLM can decide the next step. Agentic Systems covers both workflows and agents; they sit at different points on the same slider.
• "Agentic Systems" is Anthropic's umbrella term. Anthropic splits Agentic Systems into two kinds (source):
• Workflows: "systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths"
• Agents: "systems where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage"
7 · 17.9sThe RBC Assist Pro card and the Chat zone appear. The card holds a small augmented-LLM diagram (In → LLM → Out, MCP above the LLM). A dot travels through it once."CHAT" · "Single Step" · "Augmented LLM" · "RBC Assist Pro" · "MCP" · "In" · "LLM" · "Out" · "An LLM enhanced with retrieval, tools and memory"Jun's Speech• RBC Assist Pro is an in-house, horizontal platform with no domain expertise.
• One prompt goes in and one LLM response comes out. It can make tool calls, so it can connect to MCP, but there is no workflow and no loop underneath, so it cannot run a multi-step analysis.
• In Anthropic's words this is an augmented LLM: "The basic building block of agentic systems is an LLM enhanced with augmentations such as retrieval, tools, and memory." (source)
• It lets users customize an "end-user agent": a fixed prompt template plus a fixed set of MCP connections. It is still one response, so it is an augmented LLM and not an agent. (We call it a Prompt Based Agent internally. This is our own term, not an official one.)
• It fits questions and tasks that one response can answer.
• Per Anthropic it is a building block of agentic systems, not an agentic system itself, so it sits at the left end of the slider, with zero steps for the LLM to decide. It is also the smallest unit of everything on the right side: each LLM call in a workflow, and each turn of an agent, is built on it.

• Prompt Chaining is the left starting point of Agentic Systems, the pattern with the least freedom for the LLM.
• It is shown as a pattern (dashed), not as a product we have.
• Anthropic's definition of prompt chaining: "Prompt chaining decomposes a task into a sequence of steps, where each LLM call processes the output of the previous one." (source)

• It is a workflow: LLMs and tools orchestrated through predefined code paths. Every step is a node, every transition is an edge, and the process knowledge lives in code.

12 · 42.3sThe RiskMind card and an Agent bracket appear. The ReAct paper describes it:
• ReAct: "we explore the use of LLMs to generate both reasoning traces and task-specific actions in an interleaved manner" (source)
• Reasoning: "reasoning traces help the model induce, track, and update action plans as well as handle exceptions" (source)
• Acting: "actions allow it to interface with external sources, such as knowledge bases or environments, to gather additional information" (source)
• RiskMind is in-house and sits further right than DocuMind. It has domain expertise, so it is a vertical product.
• The process is written in natural language, as Skills. The Skills guide the steps, and the agent decides the next step based on that guidance. It uses scripts for the steps that must be exact.
• The number of steps is not fixed. It depends on how the Skill is written.
• Our analysis is step by step, so it could be written either way, as a workflow or as an agent. The question is which one fits what we need: expansion. Session 2 explains why.

RiskMind can do a lot of things. But if I had to summarize it in one line, RiskMind is an agent that generates risk insight from data.

We kicked off the project in April this year, and we finished the proof of concept in September. Let me walk through what we've built over those six months.		• The core message: RiskMind is an agent that generates risk insight from data, working from Skills. All numbers are calculated by code; the LLM only writes the words.
• RiskMind helps Risk Managers with analysis and risk insight. It does not replace the Official Risk Report, and Risk Managers still review what RiskMind produces.

17 · 66.4sToday, the whole segment. A white rounded card appears at the top and the whole picture shrinks to about 0.7 and sits inside it. "Risk Insight" from the positioning line flies into the right side of the card and becomes the Risk Insight node, with a small line under it for the output form. At the same time a horizontal axis is drawn under the card (drawn like the Scene 2 axis): dashed circles All Manual and Fully Automatic at the ends, a blue slider at Today (the four labels All Manual, Today, With RiskMind and Fully Automatic all sit above the axis), and a small notch at the bottom of the card pointing at it. At the end the Risk Manager and the three cards light up together."Risk Insight" · "Dashboard or Comment" · "All Manual" · "Fully Automatic" · "Today" · "Human Executes · Guided by Standard Operating Procedure" · "Risk Manager" · "Current Process" · "Official Risk Report" · "Scheduled, Automated" · "Drill Down" · "Further Analysis on Risk Report" · "Ad-hoc" · "Ad-hoc Analysis"To show how RiskMind works, let's start with how risk analysis is done in Local Market Risk today.

Risk managers produce the risk report, drill down into the drivers, and handle ad-hoc questions. The risk report is the starting point. It shows the big picture of the portfolio. Everything else builds on top of it. In the end, what we deliver is risk insight, either as a dashboard or as a comment.

Producing the risk report is already fairly automated, with Python scripts running on a schedule. But the report doesn't contain any comments. Drill-downs and ad-hoc requests still rely mostly on the risk manager doing the analysis manually.

If the desk has good documentation, the analysis steps are written down in a standard operating procedure, or SOP. It covers where to get the data, which scripts to run, and how to read the results. So today, the human executes, guided by the SOP. But an SOP isn't always there, and it isn't always up to date. So when someone moves on, the next person either follows the SOP, or has to rely on a handover from the person before them.		• Top-down analysis: the Risk Manager starts from the portfolio level (today's level and the change vs. yesterday), sees a driver, and digs into one aspect or subset to see how it drove the change.
• Ad-hoc questions may not relate to the portfolio result at all.
• The SOP is the Operational Manual the Risk Manager follows. Today the human executes, guided by the SOP.
• Both ends of the automation axis are theoretical: nobody works fully manually today, and fully automatic (no human in the loop) is not our goal.
18 · 71.5sUnder the axis an effort bar appears, as wide as the axis, running from All Manual to Fully Automatic, in three segments: Design is narrow; Execution is very long and solid; Judgement is a hatched stretch, slightly wider than Design. At the same time a pale blue beam shines down from the Today slider (like a flashlight) and covers the whole bar."Design" · "Execution" · "Judgement"The bar below shows the effort risk managers put into an analysis. Any analysis can be split into three stages. Design, execution and judgement.

Design is working out how to do the analysis, like what data you need, which analysis actually answers the question, and how to dig into the drivers. Execution is running that plan and getting the results. And judgement is validating the results and making decisions.

For most analyses, design is a one-time effort, because the questions we face keep coming back. Execution is different. It happens almost every day. So in today's process, most of the risk manager's effort goes into execution.		• The bar shows where a year of effort goes. Spotting a problem and judging whether it is worth doing is settled before RiskMind, so the bar covers only three steps: Design (designing the method), Execution, and Judgement (judging the result).
• Today: Execution is by far the largest part.
• Judgement is the Risk Manager's call on what the result means. It is not part of execution, and it stays with the Risk Manager.

Finally a right-angled line runs from Risk Insight back to the Risk Manager, labeled Verify. The bar and the slider change together: Execution shortens a lot, Design widens a little, and Judgement keeps its width; the three segments shrink and slide to the right at the same time, and the space freed on the left becomes a dashed hollow box, Saved Effort, about half of the bar. The beam starts from the slider and narrows as it moves, covering only the right-hand three segments and not Saved Effort. When the slider arrives, the notch reappears at With RiskMind. It plays straight through to Verify."With RiskMind" · "Agent Executes · Guided by Skills · Human Verifies" · "Saved Effort" · "RiskMind" · "Dashboard or Answer in Chat" · "Portfolio Analysis" · "Scheduled Service" · "Drill Down" · "Ask in Chat" · "Ad-hoc" · "Ask in Chat" · "Flags Data Issues" · "Verify"With RiskMind, we push automation further with AI. The analysis itself is much the same as today, but the way we do it is different.

RiskMind doesn't produce the official risk report. Instead, it delivers a portfolio analysis to the risk manager as a scheduled service, and that becomes the starting point. From there, the risk manager can ask follow-up questions in the chat to drill down, or ask for an ad-hoc analysis.

The agent follows Skills, which are the steps written in natural language. The result is a dashboard with comments and charts, or a direct answer in the chat. Then the risk manager verifies it.

So the process shifts from "human executes, guided by the SOP" to "agent executes, guided by Skills, human verifies". It's not just about automation. The risk manager's role changes too. With RiskMind, they design the process once, and verify the execution results every time.

Now look at what happens to the effort. Design takes a bit more. People can click through different software to get what they need, but an agent can only work through code. So some manual steps need to be automated first, and set up in a way the agent can use. But that's a one-time effort. Execution, the part we repeat every day, shrinks a lot. Judgement stays the same. It's still the risk manager's job to validate the results and make decisions. All the space that frees up on the left is the saved effort.		• Portfolio Analysis is the Risk Manager's daily starting point. It is a scheduled service that runs at a fixed time every day, so the Risk Manager does not trigger anything.
• Drill Down extends Portfolio Analysis: together they form a top-down analysis. The Risk Manager sees a driver in the portfolio result and wants to dig into one aspect or subset. They type the request in chat in natural language and specify the driver or subset.
• Ad-hoc: the Risk Manager types the question in chat in natural language. It may not relate to the portfolio result. It is in skill scope: the process must already be defined in a skill, and the agent does not write its own code or figure out the process.
• Details of how each one runs are on the "How a Pipeline Runs" slide.
• The Risk Manager always verifies RiskMind's output. RiskMind does not replace the Official Risk Report or the Risk Manager's judgment.
• The role changes: from doing the analysis every time, to designing it once and verifying it every time.
• Effort: Design takes more (more automation, and a Skill an agent follows cannot leave things implicit the way a manual for people can), but it is a one-time effort. Execution happens every run and shrinks. Judgement stays the same: it is still the Risk Manager's job. Saved Effort is everything on the left, about half the bar.

At the upper left is the User Input group (dashed frame, the User Input tile on its top edge) with three rows: Portfolio Analysis (Slash Command, Scheduled), Drill Down, Ad-hoc (Natural Language), with an arrow pointing right to the right-hand frame. Below it, the Skills folder tile unfolds into the Skill folder (its name on the frame's top edge). After the Skill appears and before the first step starts, the dashed frame on the right appears, then the Skill's arrow points at its left side (the Skill guides every step in the frame). The Skill has two parts: SKILL.md (Natural Language; the title is outside the frame) with five instructions, and Scripts (Code): analyze.py and generate_visualization.py. The Agent reads SKILL.md one instruction at a time: the current instruction highlights, the script it runs highlights with it, and the matching step unfolds on the right. Instructions 4 and 5 (generate the charts; build the dashboard with the render_html skill) both map to Build Dashboard, which moves only once. Order: Get Data (get_data MCP) → Analyze (analyze.py) → Write Comments (LLM) → Build Dashboard → Dashboard. Without stopping, a branch splits off after Analyze: Write Answer → Answer in Chat (shown only in the diagram on the right)."User Input" · "Portfolio Analysis" · "Slash Command, Scheduled" · "Drill Down" · "Ad-hoc" · "Natural Language" · "Agent" · "Executes Each Step · Guided by Skills" · "Skill" · "SKILL.md" · "Get the data through MCP." · "Run analyze.py and save the results to a file." · "Read the results and write a comment per section." · "Run generate_visualization.py for the charts." · "Build the dashboard with the render_html skill." · "Scripts" · "Code" · "analyze.py" · "generate_visualization.py" · "Get Data" · "Analyze" · "Write Comments" · "Build Dashboard" · "Dashboard" · "Write Answer" · "Answer in Chat"Now let's zoom in and see how the agent actually follows a Skill, step by step.

A request comes in, either a scheduled portfolio analysis, or a question in the chat. The agent picks it up and opens the Skill. A Skill is a folder with two parts. There's a markdown file called SKILL, with the instructions written in plain language, much like the SOP we saw earlier. And there are scripts, which are the code it can run.

The agent reads the SKILL file one instruction at a time, and does what it says. Most analyses follow a pretty standard pattern. First, it gets the data through MCP. Then it runs a script to do the calculations. Based on the results, the LLM writes the comments. Another script creates the charts, and everything is put together into a dashboard. Or, for a simple ad-hoc question, the LLM just writes the answer in the chat.		• Three pipelines, all predefined in skills. Portfolio Analysis → Drill Down is a top-down analysis.
• Pipeline summary (table below the scene).
• Portfolio Analysis: in the skill it is a slash command with parameters, so a scheduled run does not need a generated prompt. The output is a Dashboard, a self-contained HTML Artifact.
• Drill Down runs the same pipeline as Portfolio Analysis; only the scripts, the data, and the comments to write are different. The output is a Dashboard.
• Ad-hoc comes in two forms. Form 1, with a Dashboard: it runs the report flow below. Form 2, with a answer in chat: it runs the direct-answer flow below; the agent runs one script and the LLM returns the answer in chat.
• Parameters are defined in the skill. If the user leaves out a required one, the agent asks.
• The report flow, step by step:
• 1. Fetch data: the agent fetches data through MCP. The data is saved in a folder, and MCP returns only the file location.
• 2. Run scripts: scripts take the file location as input and produce a markdown file and a json file. The agent generates nothing in this step; it only executes the scripts.
• 3. Write comments: the agent reads the markdown file and the skill, then writes a comment for each section. The output is a json, with the section as the key and the comment as the value.
• 4. Visualize: a predefined script turns the data from step 2 into ECharts charts and tables. The agent does not change it. The output is a json, with the section as the key and the figure or table as the value.
• 5. Render report: the agent calls Skill: render_html, which puts each section's comment and figure together into the HTML report, one comment with one figure per section. The skill merges the comment json and the figure json by section key into a final json, renders it with a template into the HTML report, and returns the report's location to the agent.
• Why file locations are passed between steps: the agent does not need to read every file, so the data never enters the agent's context. Only what the agent needs in order to write the comments or generate the answer enters its context, and it is fed as markdown, the format the agent knows best. Everything else is digested by scripts into json. The agent does not read the json; it only passes the correct location into the next command. This keeps the agent's context as small as possible, which is the main reason the pipeline is built around file locations.
• The direct-answer flow: the agent fetches the data through MCP, runs one script, and the LLM writes the answer directly in chat. There are no comments json, figures json, or HTML report. The LLM generates only the answer.
• The next session replays this same run turn by turn to show how the agent works through it.
• In the video, steps 4 and 5 of the report flow (Visualize, Render) are shown as one step, Build Dashboard (two SKILL.md instructions, one step). The scripts shown are analyze.py (Analyze) and generate_visualization.py (charts); the dashboard is built with Skill: render_html.
• The agent decides the next step each turn, but the order of the steps is defined by the skill.
25 · 94.0sEach step changes style by who does it: Get Data, Analyze and Build Dashboard are solid blue blocks, Get Data labeled MCP, Analyze and Build Dashboard labeled Script; Write Comments and Write Answer are white boxes with a blue dashed border labeled LLM. At the end a sentence appears at the bottom."MCP" · "Script" · "LLM" · "Numbers from Scripts, Words from the LLM"Now Let's see what handles each step. MCP gets the data. Scripts do the calculations and build the dashboard. LLM only does the writing, the comments or the answer. It reads the numbers, but never calculates them, because LLM can get numbers wrong. So it's numbers from scripts, words from the LLM. Risk manager still needs to verify what it writes.• Why it is built this way: to keep the numbers accurate, the only thing generated by the LLM is the comment (or the answer in chat). Everything else is produced by scripts. The agent's job is to trigger them and keep the order right.
• The hallucination answer is the process design (code produces the numbers; the LLM writes the words), not a comparison with RBC Assist Pro.

37 · 118.6sThree dashed tools appear in the Agent row, from left to right."AutoEval" · "AutoSkill" · "AutoEvolution"While the AI champions keep adding plugins and Skills, Market Risk AI will keep working with AiXel to add more features to the platform itself. In this phase, we're planning three of them, all to help risk managers build better Skills.

AutoEval checks whether a Skill meets our standards. Going forward, every new Skill will need to pass AutoEval before it goes into RiskMind in production.

AutoSkill is an agent that helps risk managers draft Skills. Ideally, you'll be able to write a Skill just by chatting with it.

And AutoEvolution keeps improving the Skills already on RiskMind. As risk managers use a Skill, RiskMind looks back at those conversations and works out how the Skill could be better. That feedback is then used to improve the Skill.		• Skill Tooling, in order. It applies to every skill in the matrix.
• AutoEval: automatically evaluates skills, reducing our review burden.
• AutoSkill: a separate agent. The Risk Manager talks to it, and it packs the business knowledge into a skill, provides a sandbox to run it, uses AutoEval to evaluate it, and returns an evaluation report for further improvement.
• AutoEvolution: extracts feedback and critique on skills from RiskMind production runtime memory and uses it as context for the agent to enhance skills; long-term skill lifecycle management.
